subsubtopic: OVER-SEIZURE OF MONEY FROM SMALL BUSINESSWOMAN IN ST. CATHARINES, ONT.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the spirit of Ebenezer Scrooge of old, the Department of National Revenue is making life miserable for the taxpayers of St. Catharines. I have one example which is typical of many.
A woman started a small business because her husband is unemployed. Her income tax bill was $1,900. She paid $500 on account and promised to pay the balance by way of instalment payments. Revenue Canada responded by making a demand for payment in full, so she paid a further $200 on account. Then, Madam Speaker, without any forewarning whatsoever, my constituent was advised by her bank that Revenue Canada had garnisheed all the money in her savings account and in a joint checking account she had with her husband. These accounts totalled $2,049, meaning that Revenue Canada had seized almost $850 more than was owing. Some $1,300 of the money garnisheed in fact belonged to her husband.
This constituent now cannot pay her bills, let alone buy for Christmas, and Revenue Canada is estimating a six weeks wait until her money is refunded. Some Christmas my constituent will have, simply because the Minister has no control over some over zealous bureaucrat who was probably trying to make up his or her quota. This is intolerable behaviour on the part of the Department. Let the Minister clean house or resign.

Madam Speaker, today the House will be dealing with third reading of the Income Tax Bill. This is a matter which will directly affect many, many Canadians. Any tax regime must be fair and equitable amongst all the citizens exposed to such a taxation regime.
A very fundamental principle of taxation justice is that taxes by a senior level of government should not have to be paid on taxes paid to a local government. The property taxes paid on a principle place of residence to a municipal government should be deductible from income for income tax payable to senior levels of government. This is fundamental to taxation equity and justice. Indeed, limits to such deductibility up to, say, $1,000 per house per annum, increase the equity between home owners. Some will argue that such a deduction is not equitable to renters, but that is untrue because all owners of rental properties are allowed the deduction, thereby affecting the rents directly.
I am surprised that this House does not advocate and support this principle unanimously. It is certainly the case in the United States of America.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my point of order flows from yesterday's events in the House. There is little need to review the sequence of events which took place yesterday, either prior to the defeat of the Government in Committee of the Whole or after that time. What is clear is that the Committee of the Whole defeated the Government on a tax measure, one flowing directly from the November, 1981 Budget, and that the House of Commons concurred in that decision.
There is a practice and tradition stretching back to the origins of British parliamentary government whereby governments which are defeated on money Bills must seek a new mandate to govern. This Government has spurned that tradition. It has argued that there is no need for the Government to seek the confidence of the Canadian people. The Government has also argued that there is no requirement for a government to seek the confidence of the House after being defeated on a taxation issue. That, Sir, was not the position taken by the Right Hon. Lester Pearson when his Government was defeated on a taxation Bill in 1968.
Prime Minister Pearson understood that for democratic freedoms to be protected and for the rule of parliamentary law and tradition to be upheld, it was necessary to put a motion of confidence to the House. This Government does not agree with that. The Government has questioned the existence of the tradition that governments which have been defeated on money Bills have lost the confidence of the House. However, John Stewart, an ex-Liberal Member of Parliament, who served in the capacity-

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-DEFEAT IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE OF CLAUSE OF BILL C-2
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I am happy to see Government Members applauding. That Member served in the capacity of Parliamentary Secretary to the then President of the Privy Council. He was vice-chairman of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures, whose recommendations formed the basis of the 1968 rule changes. He suffered no such illusion. At page 130 of his book, The Canadian House of Commons, 1977, he said, and I quote:
But money business was different: that business put the kings' demands before reluctant members. Understandably, they wished to discuss those demands freely and fully before any decision whatsoever was taken in the House. But since then the constitution has changed. The House no longer needs to haggle with the Crown over money: if the advisers of the Crown do not have the confidence of the House, they must go.
On December 13, 1979, the Right Hon. Member from Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) had no doubts that defeat on a budgetary matter, a money matter, was an issue of confidence. It is only this Government, Sir, which fails to recognize its responsibility to Parliament and to the Canadian people to maintain and honour the practices, traditions and rules of Parliament.
There are those who would argue, Mr. Speaker, that it is up to the Government to determine what is or is not a matter of confidence. The actions of this Government speak louder than words in that regard. Clause 6 of Bill C-2 contained measures stemming from the November, 1981 Budget and votes on budgetary matters are always matters of confidence. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Government has attached such importance to this Bill, that it has delayed the consideration of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, has not proceeded with the Canada Health Act, or any other of the priorities which it set forth in the Speech from the Throne, for that matter. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, votes on the Address and Reply are confidence matters.
It is saddening to recognize, Mr. Speaker, that we are but the minority in this House and that Members opposite, with the assistance of their helpmates in the New Democratic Party, can deflect any attempt on our part to ensure that the Government is held to account for its actions in the House. This Liberal Government and its western wing in the NDP-

Because Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is in the minority in this House, both in numbers and in respect for the practices of this House, certainly as the two bedmates show, we have only two options available to us in the aftermath of yesterday's events. The first is that we can follow a procedural course that would paralyse the Government and bring about its resignation and the calling of a general election in accordance with parliamentary practice and tradition. The second option is that we could allow the business of the House to proceed while renewing our commitment to scrutinize every action of the Government and hold it accountable for its decision and its failure to govern in a responsible manner.
The best interests of this nation, Mr. Speaker, would be served if the Government were to face the electorate. However, because Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is in the minority in the House, the process of causing the Government to call an election would be a long, drawn-out procedure which would consume the time of the House and prevent the House from dealing with the very urgent problems which face this nation today. The rule of law would be served but the people of Canada would continue to face unemployment and economic and social uncertainly until the election was held. If Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition has any say in the matter, the rule of law will be defended by this House, but never at the expense of the Canadian people.

In 1968, Mr. Speaker, and this precedent was referred to yesterday, a motion for third reading of a Bill amending the Income Tax Act was defeated. The Speaker was in the chair and the vote was recorded in Votes and Proceedings. That means Journals, the only official record of proceedings. The entire Bill was defeated. The Bill represented the major segment of the Government's fiscal policy. The impact of this defeat was sufficient to induce the Government to put down a motion clarifying its position by declaring the question not to have been one of confidence. The motion was carried and the Government survived.
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
On only four occasions have Canadian Governments considered defeats to be of a confidence nature. In 1926 and 1963 governments dissolved Parliament after losing votes relating to the business of Supply, and in 1974 and 1979 governments dissolved Parliament after losing votes in the budget debate. No government has ever resigned or dissolved Parliament as a result of a vote in any committee, including Committee of the Whole. In 1979 the Clark Government lost the entire Estimates of the Department of Supply and Services in the Standing Committee and did not consider this a problem.

speechtext:
In 1967 the Pearson Government was defeated in Committee of the Whole on a resolution to raise postal rates. There was no demand for resignation or dissolution and the House immediately turned to other Government Orders. In 1973 a motion to concur in a Supplementary Estimate was defeated with the Speaker in the chair and the vote recorded in Journals. Not only was there no cry for resignation, but the House in the same sitting proceeded to vote Supply and pass two Appropriation Acts.
There are numerous occasions, Mr. Speaker, when governments as far back as Sir John A. Macdonald in the 1860s have been defeated, both in committee and with the Speaker in the chair, without considering the matter to be confidence. Sir John A. Macdonald was defeated 11 times between 1867 and 1872 in and out of committee, including defeat on a Tariff Bill. This is all listed with great detail in the very distinguished Eugene Forsey's book, which is well known, and for their knowledge I refer my colleagues to this extraordinary piece of work. There was no question of resignation or dissolution at that time either.
In Britain, Mr. Speaker, even majority governments frequently lose votes without a trace of concern about confidence. In the British House in recent years there have been dozens of defeats on all sorts of things. I would like to refer my colleagues to Professor Philip Norton's list of a string of them in The Parliamentarian, Volume LIX, page 232. The procedural authorities are silent on the question simply because it is a constitutional and not a procedural question. I think the ruling made yesterday on this point was very clear.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, one minor clause of a relieving nature in a 125-clause Bill is not a major, substantive issue. In addition, the House continued to work, passing, on a recorded division, a major motion concurring in the over-all fiscal thrust of the Government. While the Conservatives may argue that the vote confirmed the defeat of a clause in Committee of the Whole, their negative votes indicate that they did not believe that at the time.
What happened last evening, Mr. Speaker, was that a committee reported the Bill with amendments, including a deleted clause. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), seconded by myself, proposed a motion that the Bill as reported be concurred in. That Bill embodied the major fiscal thrust of the Government in the broadest sense of the word. While Votes and Proceedings, the only official record of proceedings,

We in this Party supported the view that the vote was taken properly, and that the vote taken yesterday therefore had to stand.
1 concede that there was no doubt that there were Members on both sides of the House who entered the Chamber after the vote commenced, but 1 made the point and reiterate it that it was impossible for the Chairman of the committee at that point, or for any Member, to identify the individual Members who had violated the rule. Therefore, it was impossible for the Chair to do other than to accept that the vote that had been taken and properly recorded was in fact the vote of the day.
In conjunction with that, I want to raise the point that the problem rests with the application of the rule. I have noticed over the course of the last four years that the practice in the House of Commons has been that Members have in fact entered the Chamber when the House was in Committee of the Whole and have in fact voted after the vote had commenced. However, that is in direct violation of the rules of the House of Commons.
I want to suggest that in order that such an occasion as that never arises again, we understand what the rules of the House require. Let me refer to Citation 472(3) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition which states:
As in the House during a recorded division, no Member may enter the Committee of the Whole while a division is in progress.
I would ask on behalf of my colleagues and for the sake of the sanity and orderly conduct of the House of Commons that in the future there be no such laxity permitted and that from the time the vote is called until the time the vote is recorded and announced, no Member be permitted to enter the Cham-

With respect to yesterday's proceedings, 1 want to say that I am amazed by the sudden transformation that has taken place between two o'clock yesterday and three o'clock today. At two o'clock yesterday, the Hon. Member for Yukon is recorded at page 354 of yesterday's Hansard as saying:
-since it is our view that, constitutionally, this Parliament has ceased to exist-
He goes on to explain why that is his view. Today he says that perhaps that is not really what happened, and maybe they can exercise their option to stick around and continue with the business of Parliament in the interest of the public. It almost makes one ill.
I want to suggest in closing that there was a crisis yesterday. The crisis was a parliamentary crisis and it was brought about because we in the House of Commons have not required that the rules be followed precisely. We must begin to do that. We are going to have to make sure that when we have a 15 minute bell it is a 15 minute bell; that when a Member is recognized on a point of order, it is in fact a point of order; that when Members rise on a question of privilege they state the privilege clearly which they feel has been offended; that when there are votes to be taken in Committee of the Whole, that the procedure set down in the Rules of Parliament be followed precisely, in order that occasions such as the occasion which occurred yesterday never can occur again. This sort of occurrence betrays in many ways the confidence of the public in the parliamentary system. It goes to the very root of the parliamentary system and the very fact that the people of Canada are dissatisfied with the way Parliament works. There is no wonder they do not understand it. The Members themselves do not understand it. It is time that Members of Parliament at least made the effort to understand the rules within which they operate.
I say to the Hon. Member for the Yukon that if he had had a point that would have resulted in an election being called, he would have had our support. But he had no point. He continues to operate in a dictatorial, destructive manner, ignoring other people's rights in the House of Commons, subverting everyone else's opinion to his own. I suggest the time has come to apply the Rules of Parliament to the Hon. Member for the Yukon in the same way they are applied to others.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after the Hon. Member asked his question in the House a few days ago,
I was informed that some specific amount had been set in the district office referred to by the Hon. Member, and I was also told that as soon as senior officials here in Ottawa-and that was before the Hon. Member had asked his question-were informed of the situation, they told the officials in charge of the district office that this was a practice that could not be tolerated, and they ordered that the guidelines be withdrawn.
The record of the debates of this House speaks for itself. On November 29 of this year the Minister stood in the House and said that no quota system was in use in his department. On Monday, December 19, 1983, the Minister stood in his place and said that it had come to his attention that the Kitchener office of Revenue Canada had adopted a quota system and that upon learning of the policy the Minister had ordered that it be brought to an end. Today, we have further evidence of the existence of a quota system, when only on Monday the Minister said that no quotas were in effect in other offices of Revenue Canada in other regions of the country.
Members of this House are obliged to accept the Minister on his word. Members of the House can have no doubt that he was not aware of the existence of the quota system in effect in
Kitchener when he made his November 29, 1983 statement and that he was not aware of the quotas that were brought to light in today's Question Period when he made his statement on Monday.
Section 4(1) of the Department of National Revenue Act outlines that:
The duties, powers and functions of the Minister extend and apply to the subjects and services enumerated in the schedule, over which the Minister has the control, regulation, management and supervision, subject always to the provisions of the Acts relating to the said subjects and matters connected therewith.
The Schedule to the Act includes Section 4 which stipulates that internal taxes, unless otherwise provided, including income taxes are included in the Minister's duties, powers and functions, therefore any act on the part of his departmental officials with respect to the operation of the Department which was withheld from the Minister and which caused the Minister to mislead the House constitutes a breach of the privileges of this House.
There may, of course, be some related question as to the operation of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility and the obligation of the Minister both to keep himself informed of the operations of his department and to take responsibility for the abuse of authority committed by officers of his department. Perhaps I will have the opportunity to elaborate on that point in a couple of minutes.
At the present time the House must recognize the difficulties faced by a Minister if his departmental officials do not believe it is necessary to consult with the Minister before instituting policies, or to inform him of ongoing policies within the Department. This is an unfortunate and unacceptable turn of events, but it is also one the Government must take steps to correct.
The House of Commons must decide what action should be taken when an act of omission on the part of a Minister's officials leads him to mislead the House. The telling argument, the one which was used by Mr. Speaker Jerome to determine that the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Durham, as it was then known, now the Hon. Member for Durham-Northumber-land (Mr. Lawrence), had a prima facie case of privilege, were the following words found at page 136 of the Nineteenth Edition of Erskine May:
It may be stated generally that any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any member or officer of such House in the discharge of his duty, or which has a tendency, directly or indirectly, to produce such results may be treated as a contempt even though there is no precedent of the offence.
Unlike the 1978 case raised by the Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland, the House has no evidence that the departmental officials deliberately falsified documents and thereby caused the Minister to mislead the House. However, an act of omission can have just as grievous consequences for the privileges of the House as does a deliberate act of contempt. Indeed, the failure of departmental officials to report the implementation of quotas or any other major administra-

tive policy is a contempt of Parliament, because it undermines and obstructs the Minister in the execution of his duties as outlined by an Act of this Parliament. Under Section 2(2) of the Department of National Revenue Act, the Minister is described as having the "management and direction" of the Department.
As a point of interface between the House and the Department of National Revenue, the House requires that the Minister explain and take responsibility for the policies and actions of his Department. If officers in the Department of National Revenue do not inform the Minister of their actions, he must inevitably be led to misinform and mislead the House. As May points out, this is a clear contempt of the House.
The credulity of Members of the House is stretched if we are asked to believe that the subject matter of the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North and the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead on November 29 did not come to the attention of officers of the Department of National Revenue within a few days of the time the questions were asked in the House.
At page 141 of May's Nineteenth Edition the following words may be found:
It is a breach of privilege to present or cause to be presented to either House or to committees of either House forged, falsified or fabricated documents with intent to deceive such House or committees or to subscribe the names of other persons or fictitious names to documents intended to be presented to either House or committees of either House, or to be privy to, or cognizant of, such forgery or fraud.
Surely as a result of the exchange which took place in the House between the Minister and Hon. Members on this side officials in the Department of National Revenue at some level must have become aware of the misrepresentation of the Department's policies committed in the House by the Minister. Indeed, the Minister said that he was informed by his officials of the quota system following those questions. Yet, it was not until Monday that the record was set straight. It would seem that someone or some agency within the Department was willing to allow the House to continue to be misled. Again, there would appear to have been a contempt of Parliament committed.
I would submit that certain officials of the Department of National Revenue have been guilty of causing the House to be misled. We have to accept the Minister's word that he did not deliberately mislead the House when he gave information which was later demonstrated to be untrue. Perhaps this was first an error of omission but later a direct act of contempt in allowing misleading information to remain before the House. There can be no other explanation for the fact that the Minister has put misleading and contradictory information before the House. Either knowledge had been withheld from the Minister thus leading him to mislead the House, or he deliberately misled the House.
The practice of the House is to accept Hon. Members on their word, and we do that. Therefore I can only conclude that the Minister was unaware of the actions of his Department instead of attempting to mislead us. Therefore I believe the
Privilege-Mr. Beatty
House has an obligation to investigate the matter and determine the extent of the contempt committed in this instance.
I want to return as well to the question of the Minister's behaviour. As I indicated earlier, we accept that when the Minister made his statement on November 29, in which he denied the existence of a quota system in Kitchener or in other district offices of his Department, he was telling the truth to the best of his ability. We accept that fully. We do not question his word on that. Yet, what he has told the House, as it appears on the record, is that subsequent to the question asked by the Hon. Member for Cambridge he learned from his officials that indeed the quota system alleged to be in place had in fact been in place and that subsequently officials in the Kitchener district office had been instructed to cancel it. However, an untrue statement in the Minister's name was left on the record when the true information was in the possession of officials of the Minister's Department and ultimately of the Minister himself.
When the Minister responded to questions in the House on Monday, he confessed that in fact the quota system which he previously denied existed and that he then knew about it. This clearly demonstrates that the Minister by that time had received information confirming that his statement on November 29 was false.
Also brought into question, in addition to the behaviour of officials within the Department of National Revenue, is the Minister's obligation to ensure that false statements put on the record of the House are not left to sit there. I refer again to the quotation which I earlier read from Beauchesne's which indicated that acts of omission are equally serious and can constitute contempts of the House. This was not a trivial matter.
It is often the case that Madam Speaker rules on points of orders or questions of privilege by saying that clearly a dispute as to facts has arisen during Question Period and that that does not constitute a question of privilege as such. In this case there is no dispute as to the facts. There is no dispute that the Minister on November 29, as recorded in Hansard, expressly denied the existence of a quota system in the Kitchener district office and in his Department as a whole. Further, there is no denial or disagreement on either side of the House as to the second fact, namely that subsequently the Minister learned, when his officials finally brought it to his attention, that the statement he gave was false. As a result of a question raised by the Hon. Member for Cambridge, the Minister subsequently had to concede in response that the answer he had given was wrong.
Where does this leave Members of the House in their attempt to discharge their responsibilities? This is not a frivolous matter. It was raised by my colleagues in the House of Commons because we believe that there has been a grievous assault upon the civil liberties of Canadians and that such practices within the Minister's Department seriously affect the rights of all taxpayers of Canada. This is the reason we have put it on high priority and have led it in Question Period for several days. Certainly Members on this side of the House

Privilege-Mr. Beatty
attach great seriousness to this matter. I fully accept that the Minister would as well attach great seriousness to any quota system being in place in his Department which could affect the justice with which Canadian taxpayers are treated. It is not a simple matter. It is not one which can be easily dismissed as being trivial or irrelevant.
In defence of the rights of the taxpayers of Canada, Members of Parliament have an obligation to hold the Government to account, to bring to the attention of the Government and to seek information from the Government about departmental actions which could affect those rights and to seek redress on behalf of our constituents. Indeed, that is what Hon. Members on this side were attempting to do and have attempted to do on subsequent occasions when we raised this question about the behaviour of officials of the Department of National Revenue.
If we are given false information, information which the Minister subsequently learns and concedes was false and that members of his Department clearly knew was false, then we are impeded in our ability to discharge our responsibilities as Members of Parliament. That is a clear breach of the privileges of Members of Parliament.
What is at issue here, in addition to the action and the behaviour of officials of the Department of National Revenue as to whether they kept their Minister informed, is the question of the Minister's own behaviour. One of the issues on which you, Mr. Speaker, will be asked to pass judgment is whether the Minister did not have the positive obligation to come back to the House immediately upon learning that the information he had given to the House was false to correct the record and let the truth be known.
It is apparent that there was no intention on the part of the Minister, and perhaps when he responds to this question of privilege the Minister will tell us on what date he actually became aware of the quota system in Kitchener. It is directly germane to the issue you have to consider, Mr. Speaker, namely, for how long did the Minister possess information which indicated that he misled the House of Commons? What efforts were made by the Minister? Did he attempt at the earliest possible opportunity to correct the record and ensure that misleading statements were removed from the record of Parliament and that the truth was known?
Members of the House and the public of Canada were put in the position that if it had not been for the alertness of the Hon. Member for Cambridge in coming up with documentary proof of the existence of the quota system in Kitchener which he had alleged, this House and the taxpayers of Canada would never have learned about the falseness of the Minister's statement, the fact that the Minister, albeit accidentally in ignorance, misled the House.
The Minister made no effort on his own to correct the record, set the House straight and to ensure that Members were in possession of the truth. The information was wrung out of him by my colleague for Cambridge in Question Period. Had that question not been asked and had my colleague not
been able to produce documentary evidence to prove that the Minister had misled the House, the House would never have known the truth. The Minister made no effort to discharge his responsibility to set the record straight.
Those are the two issues, the behaviour of officials of the Department of National Revenue in not informing their Minister as to matters under his jurisdiction, which left him in a position where he misled the House in the first place and, second, the responsibilities of a Minister of the Crown who has made a false statement on the record to correct it and to give Parliament the true facts. Those are the two issues upon which I am asking you to adjudicate today. If you find that I have, as I believe that I do, a prima facie question of privilege, I would be prepared to move the appropriate motion to have this matter sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for investigation and report to this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that the essence of the Hon. Member's argument that there was indeed a question of privilege revolves around the question raised by the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) who raised the issue with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) on November 19, I believe, asking the Minister whether there was a quota system, referring specifically to the Kitchener office. Subsequently a question was raised on Monday, December 19 by the Hon. Member for Cambridge asking the Minister about this issue. The Minister responded. On November 29 he indicated there was not a quota system. On December 19, he indicated:
Madam Speaker, after the Hon. Member asked his question in the House a few days ago-
That was on November 29.
-I was informed that some specific amount had been set in the district office-
In other words, a quota of some sort had been set in the district office referred to, the Kitchener office.
-and I was also told that as soon as senior officials here in Ottawa-and that was before the Hon. Member had asked his question-
That was on November 29. In October when the senior officials here in Ottawa found that a quota system of some sort had been imposed in the Kitchener office, and I continue the quote:
-and that was before the Hon. Member had asked his question were informed of the situation, they told the officials in charge of the district office that this was a practice that would not be tolerated and they ordered that the guidelines be withdrawn.
This indicates that an official or officials in the Kitchener office, prior to the time that the question was asked on November 29 by the Hon. Member for Cambridge, had put in place a local policy that did not have the approval of the regional or district offices. When the district office found out sometime in October that such a policy had been put in place by the local office, that policy was immediately quashed and the guidelines were removed. It was not, is not now, never has been, nor will it be in the future, according to the Minister, a policy of the Department of National Revenue to have quotas.
December 21, 1983

When the Hon. Member for Cambridge asked his question whether there were quotas, whether there was a policy of quotas in the Department of National Revenue, the Minister said, "No, there is not". That was at that time and is now a factual statement. The House must believe the Minister.
The Minister did not retract that statement when he made his statement on December 19, two days ago. Indeed, the Minister said: "I was informed of the practice that I have just indicated." That was in October. When he answered in November, this policy had already been quashed in the Kitchener office. It was not a national policy. Indeed, it was quashed at the insistence of the Ottawa officials when they found out that such a practice was taking place.
The Minister did not mislead the Hon. Member for Cambridge when he asked this question on November 29 because the practice had been quashed in October. The question was whether there is or was a quota system. No, there is not. The fact is there was not. There was not such a policy at the national level. It was not then being practised in Kitchener because as soon as the Ottawa office found out about it in October, the program was stopped on the spot.
On November 29 when the Minister said: "No, there was not", there was not. When the Minister responded in December, he elaborated upon his answer to the Hon. Member for Cambridge. He said that he was informed that there was some specific amount and subsequent to his November 29 statement his officials indicated what the facts were surrounding this situation.
Immediately on being asked the question, the Minister brought forth information that indeed such a practice had been put in place in a local office, that it was not National Revenue policy and as soon as Department of National Revenue officials found out about it it was stopped. As soon as the question was raised in the House and the Minister made his statement, which was factual, and his officials brought it to his attention, he brought it to the attention of the Hon. Member for Cambridge saying: that, yes, in one local office this had been put in place without authority, without authorization and as soon as it was found out, it was stopped, and it is not National Revenue policy.
The Minister did not mislead the House intentionally or unintentionally on November 29. The Minister did not mislead the House intentionally or unintentionally on December 19. The grounds that the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) is using for a question of privilege is that the Minister unintentionally misinformed the House on November 29, and because he did not bring something to the attention of the House which the Hon. Member for Welling-ton-Dufferin-Simcoe alleges was in his possession prior to December 19, that somehow this act of omission means that there is a question of privilege in the actions of the Minister of National Revenue.
First, the November 29 statements were not incorrect. He did not mislead the Hon. Member for Cambridge in any way based on the question asked and the answer given. As a result, there was no omission and there was no commission. On the
Petitions
basis of the factual evidence, the answers given by the Minister, the facts that surround the situation in the Kitchener office and the fact that it was not National Revenue policy- indeed that was the essence of the question of the Hon. Member for Cambridge, whether it was National Revenue policy to have a quota system-the Minister answered factually and answered honestly. He has not misled the House in any way, shape or form. As a result of that, the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe has no grounds whatsoever for a question of privilege.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roy MacLaren (for Mr. Lalonde) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-2, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to make related amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I was saying just a moment ago that some of our colleagues have asked me and the others who will participate in this debate to be brief in our observations in this final consideration of the Bill. They have done so because they are eager, as I understand it, to catch airplanes to their homes for the Christmas holiday. I will certainly bear their needs very much in mind in my remarks and attempt to be brief about a Bill which, however, does attract considerable comment, largely because it is a vehicle for the Government's initiatives to promote investment and produce growth in our private sector as one of the answers to the problems of economic recovery, and particularly unemployment, which have faced Canada in recent times.
Bill C-2 arises out of the Budget of April, 1983 where the directions which are now expressed in this tax legislation were set forth. I regret, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of our rather bizarre proceedings yesterday we have a Bill before us which does not contain a clause which would have had the effect of providing some benefit to Canadians who were earning interest income on annuities or certain insurance policy income.
How would it benefit them?

Clause 6, which is no longer in the Bill, deals with subsection 12.2(4) of the Income Tax Act. That subsection permits individuals to report accrued annuity and certain insurance policy income annually instead of every three years.
It is still there.
This a relieving rule to allow individuals to report smoother income and get better use of the $1,000 annual investment income exemption.
It is still there. That is what Clause 4 says.

Clause 6 makes three very technical, clarifying and relieving amendments to the subsection of the Income Tax Act which I have already noted. First, it simply clarifies that this annual election is not available to corporations. This is strictly technical-

That is right. It imposes a higher tax.

December 21, 1983
Income Tax Act

-as under the existing law corporations are required to be on an annual reporting basis. They do not have a three-year rule, just a one-year rule, so there is no substantive change there. Second, it contains a relieving rule to ensure that annual reporting is available with respect to annuities under which payments have commenced, not only for deferred annuities, as is the case under the existing law. Finally, the amendment would have provided for a different mechanism to elect to treat certain annuities as prescribed annuities not subject to either annual or triennial accrual relieving.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I find it strange that the Official Opposition would have set its face against such a clause in the Bill which can bring some benefit to some Canadians, relieving them of some tax imposition which now, unfortunately, they will incur. I will leave it to Opposition members to indicate why it was that they set themselves against such a beneficial clause in the Bill. 1 cannot imagine what their motives could possibly have been.
Turning to the broader substance of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, I wanted to say that I have been impressed with the quality of some of the discussion during our review of the legislation. I have listened carefully to the concerns which were expressed by some Hon. Members. I have in mind, for example, the comments made by Hon. Members with respect to the complexity of the tax legislation. I feel it is a fair observation to say that, as a result of our discussion, it is evident that Hon. Members on all sides of the House are concerned about the complexity of current tax legislation. I, for one, certainly hope it will be possible for us to make some progress in that area as a result of the initiatives the Government has taken over the past year or so to identify ways in which our present tax legislation can be simplified, particularly in the case of small businesses.
What 1 would like to say a word about this afternoon is under three headings; first, the changes to the income tax proposed in the April Budget; second, the indexed securities investment plan-ISIP-and, third, the proposals for changes to tax incentives for research and development, a subject which unfortunately we did not have the opportunity to touch on yesterday because of the curious proceedings of yesterday afternoon.
On the question of the major tax measures flowing from the April Budget, I would want to note in particular that the underlying purpose of those measures was to accelerate productive investment and job creation in our private sector. To that end, the Bill improves the effectiveness of the investment tax credit. It provides that credits earned for eligible investment made after April 19 may be used without limit to reduce federal income tax payable. This is a new procedure in Canada and one which will be of real benefit to many businesses, many corporations. Unused credits may be carried over for deduction in any one of three previous or seven subsequent years.
The extension of the investment tax credit to heavy equipment in the construction industry will be of further benefit. The measures which we have put into the Bill to encourage new expenditure by businesses not currently paying income tax
includes two further incentives: first, a portion of the investment tax credit resulting from expenditures made after April 19 and before May 1, 1986 will be refunded to the business incurring the expenditure. For small business corporations and unincorporated businesses, 40 per cent of the investment tax credits not used to reduce income taxes will be refundable, adding to the cash flow of such companies and allowing them to overcome some of the cash difficulties which they have encountered during the recent period of recession.
I could note a number of other measures, Mr. Speaker. For instance, there is the special recovery share-purchase tax credit which will allow corporations with unused investment tax credits to flow out their credits to investors and thereby attract more equity capital into companies which have encountered, in many instances, quite serious debt-equity ratio problems in the last year or year and a half. I want, however, to spend a moment on the question of losses in that business sector which will now be eligible to be carried back for three years and forward for seven years, instead of the one year back and five years forward under existing legislation. This will be of real benefit to small businesses, including farmers and fishermen who will be immediately entitled to a three-year carryback and a ten-year carryforward of losses.
I touched for a moment on measures intended to attract additional investment into Canadian companies both small and medium-sized. However, I also want to note merely in passing the ISIP program of which we had substantial discussion in the last day. That program is, of course, intended to immunize that portion of capital gains which are inflation created. We want to ensure that Canadians investing a portion of their savings in the common equity of Canadian corporations realize real benefits and are not taxed on an inflated benefit. We are doing this to attract a larger share of the savings of Canadians into common equity than has generally been the case in Canada. The cost to the federal Treasury in the next four years will begin to become substantial but we consider this a well worth while investment to encourage greater and more widespread equity investment by individual Canadians.
The third area I want to touch on, Mr. Speaker, relates to research and development. As a government we produced a consultative paper tabled with the Budget in April offering new methods of channelling funds, incentives in the private sector to companies engaging in research and development, either in its application or in design and initiative. I will not go into the details, but it will simplify the way in which firms will be able to develop their research programs and benefit from the increasing emphasis in our economy today on the need to engage in research and development and in the application of high technology in our industry.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, one word about personal taxation. Members will realize we have offered under the RHOSP plan additional incentives to Canadians to own their own homes, to purchase new homes before the end of 1984, and we offered as
December 21, 1983

a short-term incentive during 1983 support for the purchase of certain designated home furnishings and appliances.
On the personal taxation side as well, we have increased the employment expense deduction which will move from 3 per cent to 20 per cent of employment income, subject to the current maximum amount of $500. About four million employees across Canada whose annual employment income is below $16,700 will benefit from that measure. The child tax credit has been maintained at $343 for the 1983 fiscal year, but will continue to be fully indexed to the inflation rate in subsequent years. The ceiling on the child care expense deduction will be doubled to $2,000 per child and a maximum of $8,000 per family.
We have taken these measures in recognition of the particular needs of families in our society. They, to a degree, render more complex the tax system, as all such measures do, but we felt that they were required and needed as Canada emerges from a period of recession along with the other industrialized countries of the world. We welcome the support the Bill has received. I look forward to hearing from my colleagues, and I trust my friends from western Canada who are eager to be on their way will realize that all of us will remain brief in our comments so as to allow them to continue with their plans.

speechtext: Guess who did that yesterday?

Mr. Speaker, it is a Bill for the brokers because the ISIP program makes sure that those who trade in listed stocks are able to pay only half-rate taxes on their trading income. Yesterday the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) was asked by my colleague for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) whether brokers can be involved in an ISIP with something like 2,400 or 4,800 trades. The Minister said "Of course they can". That is right because if you are in the business of trading in stocks options, of wheeling and dealing in the stock market and of not investing but buying and selling, then you can put your deals behind an ISIP and you only pay a 50 per cent tax rate on it because it is treated as a capital gain. But if you are an ordinary fellow who runs a business such as buying and selling vegetables, you have to pay 100 per cent taxes on your profits. It depends on who you are and who you know.
There used to be a Liberal Party in this country that believed in fairness and equity. This Government believes in treating stock brokers and traders and wheelers and dealers in the marketplace as preferred people. This Government makes sure it hammers the ordinary people in business. We have had question after question regarding how they hammer the little peole, the farmers and businessmen, with their Department of National Revenue and their Gestapo. Yet in this Bill they do something for the brokers.

December 21, 1983
Income Tax Act
Let us go on to what they claim they are doing for R and D to stimulate investment. They organize a system in this Bill where investment tax credits can be passed off to investors. The company cannot use them. The company can only carry them back or carry them forward, but the investors can have the tax credit. The money cannot be somehow paid to the company to help its balance sheet. The investors get the tax credits.
This Bill is an iniquitous Bill. It is an attempt to handle regional disparity. There is a series of stupid sections. If you do R and D in the Gaspe you get a 30 per cent tax credit. If you do R and D in Brampton, Ontario you get a 20 per cent tax credit. Can you tell me if Northern Telecom is going to build a plant in the Gaspe for an extra 10 per cent of tax credit which in fact comes off their deductions in writing off expenses anyway? Who is kidding whom? That is a lot of nonsense.
It is a poorly drafted Bill. The Minister knows the Bill is not worth a tinker. The Bill is designed for the tax consultants. The Bill is designed to make the income tax law so complicated that no one can read the Bill. We have now new forms of corporate tax, Part VII tax and Part VIII tax. They cannot read the Bill. We voted against Clause 6 in the Bill. We have just had an explanation from the Minister about Clause 6. The fact is that their press releases say that it hurts people not to have that clause. The only people who are hurt are the tax bureaucrats and this Government, its prestige and its right to govern. This Government must resign.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 feel somewhat peculiar speaking today on this Bill. There are in excess of one million Canadians sitting at home jobless today. We have real interest rates approaching record high levels in the country. We have businesses which tell us that next year their investment is going to be down from this year, which was down from last year and down from the year before. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the recession is going to continue in 1984.
In some parts of the country we are experiencing depressionlike conditions. On virtually the eve of Christmas the Government says to the people of Canada: "We have got a Christmas present for you: we are going to increase your taxes". That is the kind of Christmas news the people of Canada are getting in the dying moments of this session before Christmas, 1983. That is the approach of the Grinch who stole Christmas. The Minister of State for Finance is taking on the stature of Caesar Agustus II. Nine hundred and eighty-four years ago:
It came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed-
And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city.
And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem;... to be taxed-
What we are seeing here, Mr. Speaker, is a repeat of an incident which occurred many years ago where a very wicked dictator decided to provide a present to the people of the Roman Empire and imposed a tax on everyone. There is a
good side to this Bill. By increasing taxes to middle and lower income Canadians in all parts of Canada the Bill acts as a unifying force. It brings together people from all over Canada, men and women who speak English, French and other languages, unified against a Government that has shown itself to be the most heartless Government that we have seen in many, many decades.
I am not going to go on today, Mr. Speaker, as I would like-
Good.

Well, perhaps I will go on for a little longer on the prompting of my friends in the Conservative Party who would like to hear more. I would like to take a moment or two to point out some of the incredible aspects of this Bill which the Government wants us to pass with haste. There are going to be some people in this country who benefit. Some people in this country are going to be very happy. I am talking about a handful of people who use the stock market as speculators and play with the stock market. Those people are going to be benefiting considerably. As an example, under a clause which we call ISIP, if a person makes a capital gain of $60 in the course of a year, that individual would have to report in a given year an income of $15. This would be taxable at 50 per cent, which would be $7.50. The tax rate is 50 per cent. Therefore, the tax payable on income of $60 from the stock market would be $3.75. That is a tax rate of 6 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the first year.

If the Liberal Government was giving all Canadians a 6 per cent tax rate in one year on an investment of $60 for a Christmas present, people would be pleased to get that. The ISIP clause is going to cost Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars. Middle and low-income Canadians will have to pay for the tax loopholes. We now have 200 tax loopholes in our tax system.
On top of that the Government says; "We have another surprise for the people of Canada just before Christmas. We are going to increase the federal sales tax so that everybody who buys goods across this country will have an opportunity to pay another percentage point in federal sales tax". Mr. Speaker, this is coming at a time when we are in a deep recession and people are struggling to survive. The answer of members of the Liberal Party is to increase taxes.
The Canadian ownership special charge is a levy of 4.5 cents per gallon which was placed on gasoline to enable Petro-Canada to purchase Petrofina. That was done. Perhaps I will elaborate on this point for the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). Obviously he wants to hear more about this particular point so I will continue.
The Canadian ownership special charge will cost Canadian taxpayers $965 million next year, $985 million the following year and in excess of $1 billion the next year. That is the kind of legislation with which we are dealing in the House. Further-
December 21, 1983

more, we could talk about the 6 per cent on telecommunications services that has been levied, which means every time we pay our cable companies we will be paying 6 per cent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
In September the Government increased the excise tax on alcohol not by 6 per cent or 5 per cent but by 13.3 per cent. It increased the excise tax on tobacco by 15.8 per cent. Finally, as the culmination of it all, the Government said it will remove what I suppose is the only tax loophole, if one can call it that, which is the $100 deductible for charitable organizations. It said that it would eliminate that provision as well which will perhaps take $85 million away from the charities of Canada.
1 want to add one particular point which has been overlooked. It is that the Government has gone on at some length, leading up to today, talking about the child tax credit. It was $326 and the Government said it would give a magnificent increase up to $343. Big deal! Nevertheless, it is a minor increase. It will cost the Government $95 million over the next four years.
What the Government did not tell us was that it was going to hold to the 1981 family income threshold which will allow it to take in $335 million. When these amounts are figured out, it means that the Government will have a net gain of $240 million a year as a result of changes to the child tax credit. It does not tell us about matters of that sort.
I will conclude my short speech this afternoon by reminding Hon. Members opposite that when they stand in a few minutes to support this Bill they are supporting a tax system that enables thousands of Canadians who make in excess of $50,000, $60,000 and $100,000 a year to pay not a single penny in income tax, while most Canadians across the country who have their wages and salaries deducted at source must make up for the loopholes that are created. For example, of those who make an income in the $50,000 per year bracket, 8,031 did not pay any income tax last year. Of those in the $100,000 to $150,000 bracket, 793 did not pay a simple penny in income tax. Of those few individuals who made well over a quarter of a million dollars in income last year, 239 did not pay a single penny in income tax. I think it is the best example that I can think of to support the saying: "Those who pay the piper call the tune". Those who contribute to the election coffers of the Liberal Party, and I suspect to the Conservative Party as well, are certainly getting the benefits of the tax system made even more beneficial on their behalf.
I want to conclude by making a plea to the Minister of State for Finance. We have all co-operated to get this Bill through quickly. We have all co-operated and made sacrifices in terms of what many Members wanted to do with this Bill in order to allow it to be dealt with today. I would ask the Minister of State for Finance to take steps to ensure that the Department of National Revenue has adequate staff to ensure that the tax returns for 1983 will be processed on time, that some people will not have to wait until October or November to receive the refunds which are due to them, and so that the term "many happy returns" takes on an additional meaning for 1983.
